quests.question: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a simple participle phrase, unlike clauses with 'who' or 'which'?
quests.hint: Reduction works by dropping a subject relative pronoun and a form of 'be' - does 'where' introduce that same kind of clause?
quests.explanation: 'Where' clauses show place, not a subject performing or receiving an action, so they don't reduce to a participle phrase the way 'who' or 'which' subject clauses do.
options: Both can be reduced the same way.
The town where my grandmother was born has hardly changed.
Neither can be reduced.
The town founded in 1850 has hardly changed.
quests.correctAnswer: The town where my grandmother was born has hardly changed.

quests.question: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.hint: Ask whether the clause shows a time, or a subject doing or receiving an action.
quests.explanation: 'When' clauses show time, not a subject performing or receiving an action, so, like 'where' clauses, they resist this kind of reduction.
options: The year when the company was founded is engraved on the plaque.
Neither can be reduced.
The plaque engraved with the founding year hangs in the lobby.
Both can be reduced the same way.
quests.correctAnswer: The year when the company was founded is engraved on the plaque.

quests.question: Which of these relative clause types CAN be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.hint: Think back across everything covered so far in this phase - which single category of clause has consistently allowed reduction?
quests.explanation: Only subject relative clauses introduced by 'who,' 'which,' or 'that' reduce to a participle phrase; clauses with 'where,' 'when,' 'whose,' and object relative clauses generally cannot.
options: Clauses with 'whose'
Subject relative clauses with 'who,' 'which,' or 'that'
Object relative clauses
Clauses with 'where' or 'when'
quests.correctAnswer: Subject relative clauses with 'who,' 'which,' or 'that'

quests.question: The house that is being renovated will sell for more. Which is the correctly reduced form?
quests.hint: The original clause shows an action in progress and passive - which reduced form keeps both of those meanings?
quests.explanation: 'Being renovated' keeps both the passive voice and the ongoing sense of 'that is being renovated'; simply saying 'renovated' would suggest the work is already finished.
options: The house renovated will sell for more.
The house that being renovated will sell for more.
The house being renovated will sell for more.
The house renovating will sell for more.
quests.correctAnswer: The house being renovated will sell for more.

quests.question: Compare: A) 'The proposal being reviewed by the board...' B) 'The proposal reviewed by the board...' Which one means the review is STILL happening right now?
quests.hint: One version keeps the sense of an action in progress; the other suggests the action is already finished.
quests.explanation: 'Being reviewed' shows the review is currently in progress. 'Reviewed' alone suggests the review has already been completed.
options: Sentence A
Neither sentence
Sentence B
Both sentences equally
quests.correctAnswer: Sentence A

quests.question: The patients ___ treated in the emergency room require immediate attention.
quests.hint: This describes patients currently undergoing treatment, in a passive and ongoing sense - which word captures both?
quests.explanation: 'Being treated' reduces 'who are being treated,' correctly keeping the ongoing, passive meaning.
options: be
been
who being
being
quests.correctAnswer: being

quests.question: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Why does this sentence feel confusing on a first read?
quests.hint: Try reading it as: 'The horse [that was] raced past the barn fell.' Does that help it make more sense?
quests.explanation: This is a classic 'garden path' sentence: readers first interpret 'raced' as the main verb, then hit 'fell' and must backtrack to realize 'raced past the barn' is a reduced passive clause describing which horse fell.
options: 'Barn' should be 'barn's' to show possession.
'Raced' looks like the main verb at first, but it's actually a reduced passive clause modifying 'horse,' and 'fell' is the real main verb.
The sentence is simply ungrammatical and has no correct reading.
'Fell' is a typo for 'feel.'
quests.correctAnswer: 'Raced' looks like the main verb at first, but it's actually a reduced passive clause modifying 'horse,' and 'fell' is the real main verb.

quests.question: 'The suspect questioned by police confessed.' What is 'questioned by police' doing in this sentence?
quests.hint: Ask who questioned whom - did the suspect do the questioning, or receive it?
quests.explanation: 'Questioned by police' is a reduced passive clause modifying 'the suspect'; the real main verb is 'confessed.'
options: It shows that the suspect questioned the police.
It's a reduced passive clause describing 'the suspect' - the suspect was questioned by police.
It's the main verb of the sentence.
It's an error and should be removed.
quests.correctAnswer: It's a reduced passive clause describing 'the suspect' - the suspect was questioned by police.

quests.question: Which rewrite avoids the initial confusion of 'The results collected during the trial surprised the researchers,' while keeping the same meaning?
quests.hint: The original could be briefly misread as 'the results collected the trial' before 'surprised' arrives - which rewrite removes that momentary confusion most simply?
quests.explanation: Restoring the full clause 'that were collected during the trial' removes any chance of misreading 'collected' as the main verb.
options: The results, that were collected during the trial, surprised the researchers.
The results collecting during the trial surprised the researchers.
The results collected during the trial surprising the researchers.
The results that were collected during the trial surprised the researchers.
quests.correctAnswer: The results that were collected during the trial surprised the researchers.

quests.question: The report prepared by the analyst and reviewed by two directors was finally approved. How many reduced clauses does this sentence contain?
quests.hint: Look for each participle that could expand back into 'that was ___' - count them separately.
quests.explanation: There are two reduced clauses joined by 'and': 'prepared by the analyst' and 'reviewed by two directors,' both describing 'the report.'
options: None
One
Three
Two
quests.correctAnswer: Two

quests.question: Expand fully: 'The employees hired last year and trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.'
quests.hint: Both participles are passive - check that the expanded version uses the passive voice for each.
quests.explanation: 'Hired' and 'trained' are both past participles showing passive meaning, so both expand to 'who were': 'who were hired ... and who were trained ...'
options: The employees whose hired last year and trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.
The employees hiring last year and training by senior staff outperformed expectations.
The employees who were hired last year and who were trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.
The employees who hired last year and who trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.
quests.correctAnswer: The employees who were hired last year and who were trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.

quests.question: The team leading the project and impressed by the results celebrated together. What might feel slightly unusual about this sentence, and why?
quests.hint: Check whether the team is doing the leading (active) and doing or receiving the impressing (passive) - are both readings logically correct here?
quests.explanation: The team actively leads the project ('leading') but passively receives the impression from the results ('impressed by the results') - both meanings are logically correct, even though mixing voices in one sentence can feel stylistically a little busy.
options: 'Impressed' should be replaced with 'impressing' to match 'leading.'
'Leading' should be replaced with 'led' to match 'impressed.'
It mixes an active reduction ('leading') with a passive one ('impressed'), which is grammatical but can feel stylistically unbalanced.
It is completely ungrammatical and must be rewritten.
quests.correctAnswer: It mixes an active reduction ('leading') with a passive one ('impressed'), which is grammatical but can feel stylistically unbalanced.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly describes an email that SOMEONE ELSE is currently drafting?
quests.hint: The email isn't drafting itself - someone else is drafting it, and the action is ongoing. Which participle shows both?
quests.explanation: 'Being drafted' correctly shows the passive, ongoing relationship: my assistant is currently drafting the email.
options: Both sentences mean the same thing.
The email drafted my assistant needs your approval before noon.
The email drafting my assistant needs your approval before noon.
The email being drafted by my assistant needs your approval before noon.
quests.correctAnswer: The email being drafted by my assistant needs your approval before noon.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly combines these facts: 'The satellite was launched in 2019. The satellite's data has transformed weather forecasting.'
quests.hint: The 'whose' clause must stay in full and unreduced; only check whether the rest of the sentence is grammatical.
quests.explanation: 'Whose data has transformed weather forecasting' correctly keeps the possessive clause intact, since 'whose' clauses cannot be reduced to a participle phrase.
options: The satellite, whose data has transformed weather forecasting, was launched in 2019.
The satellite data transformed weather forecasting was launched in 2019.
The satellite whose data transforming weather forecasting was launched in 2019.
The satellite, data transforming weather forecasting, was launched in 2019.
quests.correctAnswer: The satellite, whose data has transformed weather forecasting, was launched in 2019.

quests.question: Which sentence is grammatically flawed?
quests.hint: A reduced clause never keeps its relative pronoun - check whether any option has accidentally kept one alongside a participle.
quests.explanation: 'Who overseeing' incorrectly combines a relative pronoun with a reduced participle; it should read either 'who oversees three departments' or simply 'overseeing three departments,' never both together.
options: The manager, who overseeing three departments, rarely takes a lunch break.
The volunteers organizing the event meet every Tuesday.
The bridge, damaged in the storm, remains closed to traffic.
The funds raised at the gala will support the shelter.
quests.correctAnswer: The manager, who overseeing three departments, rarely takes a lunch break.

quests.question: Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.hint: Check whether each pronoun matches its grammatical job - subject, object, or possession.
quests.explanation: 'Which employees voted' incorrectly uses 'which' where possession is intended; the employees belong to the company, so 'whose employees voted' is correct.
options: The book that inspired the film was written decades ago.
The company which employees voted for new benefits announced the change.
The engineer who designed the bridge received an award.
The nurse who treated me was very kind.
quests.correctAnswer: The company which employees voted for new benefits announced the change.

quests.question: Which of these sentences misuses a relative pronoun?
quests.hint: Check whether the object pronoun in each sentence matches a person or a thing.
quests.explanation: 'Whom the board rejected' should refer to a person, but here it wrongly refers to 'the proposal,' a thing; 'which the board rejected' is correct.
options: The witness whose testimony was crucial has been located.
The proposal whom the board rejected needs revision.
The technician who repaired the printer left early.
The client whom we contacted twice never responded.
quests.correctAnswer: The proposal whom the board rejected needs revision.

quests.question: In a formal legal filing, which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.hint: This is a formal legal document - check each object pronoun against the stricter, formal standard.
quests.explanation: In formal legal writing, an object pronoun for a person should be 'whom,' not 'who': 'the court found the plaintiff liable,' so 'the plaintiff' is the object and needs 'whom.'
options: The witness whom the defense cross-examined changed her account.
The judge whose ruling was overturned declined to comment.
The plaintiff who the court found liable has filed an appeal.
The evidence that was presented remains under seal.
quests.correctAnswer: The plaintiff who the court found liable has filed an appeal.

quests.question: Which sentence contains an omission error?
quests.hint: Check whether each clause that needs its own subject actually has one.
quests.explanation: 'Missed the deadline' has no subject of its own - 'the employee' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'who missed the deadline.'
options: The password I reset still isn't working.
The employee missed the deadline apologized to the team.
The client we contacted responded quickly.
The invoice we received yesterday needs review.
quests.correctAnswer: The employee missed the deadline apologized to the team.
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted

quests.question: Which sentence has wrongly dropped its relative pronoun?
quests.hint: Check each clause set off by commas - does it still have a visible connecting word?
quests.explanation: 'This contract, we finally signed' drops the pronoun inside a non-defining clause, which is never allowed; it should read 'which we finally signed.'
options: This contract, we finally signed, took months to negotiate.
The clauses that concerned us most were removed.
The contract we finally signed took months to negotiate.
The lawyer who drafted it charged a flat fee.
quests.correctAnswer: This contract, we finally signed, took months to negotiate.
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun

quests.question: Which sentence contains an error involving an unnecessary relative pronoun?
quests.hint: Look for a sentence where a word like 'that' has been inserted even though nothing in the sentence needs a describing clause.
quests.explanation: 'I finally fixed that the leak yesterday' incorrectly inserts 'that' into what should be a simple sentence with no relative clause at all.
options: The plumber who fixed it charged extra for the emergency call.
I finally fixed the leak.
I finally fixed that the leak yesterday.
The leak I finally fixed had been dripping for weeks.
quests.correctAnswer: I finally fixed that the leak yesterday.

quests.question: Which of these sentences has a mistake?
quests.hint: Match each relative word to its antecedent's category - is it a place, a time, a reason, or a person?
quests.explanation: 'The reason where she left' incorrectly pairs 'where' with 'the reason'; it should be 'the reason why she left,' since 'why' is the relative adverb of reason.
options: The colleague who trained me has since retired.
The station where we said goodbye still feels quiet to me.
The year when everything changed is one I'll never forget.
The reason where she left the company was never explained.
quests.correctAnswer: The reason where she left the company was never explained.

quests.question: Which sentence below is not grammatical?
quests.hint: Ask whether any relative adverb here is being forced to act as the subject of its own clause - something adverbs can never do.
quests.explanation: 'Why frustrated every passenger' incorrectly uses 'why' as the subject of 'frustrated'; relative adverbs can never serve as a clause's subject.
options: The delay why frustrated every passenger was never explained.
The gate where passengers waited was overcrowded.
The morning when the flight was cancelled was chaotic.
The delay that frustrated every passenger was never explained.
quests.correctAnswer: The delay why frustrated every passenger was never explained.

quests.question: One of these sentences breaks a grammar rule - which one?
quests.hint: Check what the verb inside the clause needs - a location to happen in, or a direct object to receive the action.
quests.explanation: 'Selected' takes 'the venue' as its direct object - the company selected the venue itself, not a location - so 'which' is needed, not 'where.'
options: The venue where we celebrated was fully booked months in advance.
The office where I work has a rooftop garden.
The park where the festival takes place is closed for repairs.
The venue where the company selected for the gala impressed every guest.
quests.correctAnswer: The venue where the company selected for the gala impressed every guest.

quests.question: Which sentence contains a punctuation error, given that the speaker has only one sister?
quests.hint: One sister means this clause is extra information - check the commas.
quests.explanation: Since there is only one sister, 'who lives in Berlin' is non-defining and needs commas on both sides; without them, the sentence wrongly implies the speaker has several sisters.
options: My sister who lives in Berlin is visiting next month.
My mother, who taught me to cook, passed down her recipes.
My neighbor, whose garden is famous locally, won an award.
The recipe that she gave me is a family secret.
quests.correctAnswer: My sister who lives in Berlin is visiting next month.

quests.question: Which sentence contains a punctuation error?
quests.hint: Check which relative pronoun is never allowed to follow a comma.
quests.explanation: 'That' can never introduce a non-defining clause; since the Amazon River is unique, this clause needs 'which,' not 'that.'
options: The treaty that governs the river was signed in 1978.
Rivers that flow through multiple countries often have complex water treaties.
The Amazon River, that is the largest river by discharge volume, flows through Brazil.
The Amazon River, which is the largest river by discharge volume, flows through Brazil.
quests.correctAnswer: The Amazon River, that is the largest river by discharge volume, flows through Brazil.

quests.question: A safety notice says: 'Workers, who operate heavy machinery, must wear ear protection.' Why is this punctuation likely a mistake?
quests.hint: Think about who the notice is actually meant to apply to - all workers, or only some of them.
quests.explanation: The commas turn the clause into extra, non-defining information, wrongly implying every worker operates heavy machinery. Without commas, the clause would correctly limit the rule to workers who operate such machinery.
options: The commas make the clause non-defining, incorrectly implying that all workers operate heavy machinery.
'Who' should be replaced with 'whom' in this sentence.
There is no error; the punctuation is correct as written.
The sentence needs a semicolon instead of commas.
quests.correctAnswer: The commas make the clause non-defining, incorrectly implying that all workers operate heavy machinery.

quests.question: Which sentence contains a preposition error?
quests.hint: Check which relative pronoun is allowed to follow a preposition directly.
quests.explanation: 'Who' can never follow a preposition; after 'with,' a person requires 'whom': 'with whom I share an office.'
options: The manager to whom I report is based abroad.
The colleague with who I share an office is retiring.
The colleague with whom I share an office is retiring.
The colleague I share an office with is retiring.
quests.correctAnswer: The colleague with who I share an office is retiring.

quests.question: Which sentence here is not correctly formed?
quests.hint: Count how many times the preposition appears - it should belong in only one place.
quests.explanation: 'In which we grew up in' uses the preposition twice, once fronted and once stranded; only one of the two positions should be used.
options: The house which we grew up in was sold last year.
The house we grew up in was sold last year.
The house in which we grew up in was sold last year.
The house in which we grew up was sold last year.
quests.correctAnswer: The house in which we grew up in was sold last year.

quests.question: Which sentence is completely free of errors?
quests.hint: Check pronoun choice, comma placement, and whether any clause structure has been doubled or broken across all four options.
quests.explanation: This option correctly uses a defining clause ('who guided my thesis') to identify the advisor, followed by a non-defining clause ('whom I met with regularly') adding extra detail, with punctuation and pronouns both correct throughout.
options: The advisor, whom I met with regularly, that guided my thesis has retired.
The advisor whose guided my thesis met with regularly has retired.
The advisor who I met with regularly guided my thesis, has retired.
The advisor who guided my thesis, whom I met with regularly, has retired.
quests.correctAnswer: The advisor who guided my thesis, whom I met with regularly, has retired.
